brand.subtitle: Knowledge Check — Introduction to CTFS - For TechIQ Attendees

questions.question: How many CTFS modules are there in the platform?
choices: Three modules: GrantPlan, Contracting, and Site Payments
Five modules: GrantPlan, Contracting, Forecasting, Site Payments, and one more
Four modules covering budgeting, contracts, payments, and forecasting
Six modules including a new analytics module launching in 2026
questions.feedback_correct: You've got it—the five modules are GrantPlan, Contracting, Forecasting, Site Payments, and one additional module that completes the financial backbone.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The platform includes five distinct modules that work together to create the unified financial lifecycle. The instructor notes on Slide 10 lay out all five clearly.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes what happens when a contract is signed in CTFS Contracting?
choices: The contract is stored securely and sent to the site for their records
Payment milestones in Site Payments are automatically informed, and budget alignment in GrantPlan updates without manual re-entry
A manual review process is triggered to verify contract terms against the budget
The contract data must be re-entered into the Site Payments system by the finance team
questions.feedback_correct: Exactly—that's the integration power of CTFS. The signed contract automatically triggers downstream systems, eliminating manual data transfer.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The key insight is that Contracting is not standalone. When a CTA is signed, it automatically informs payment milestones and updates budget alignment—no re-entry required. That's what separates CTFS from point solutions.

questions.question: What is the primary pain point that Contracting module solves?
choices: Sites are unable to access contract documents electronically
Contract execution is manual, error-prone, and delays site activation and payments
Sponsors cannot track which contracts have been fully executed
Legal teams lack visibility into amendment history and approval workflows
questions.feedback_correct: That's right—the Contracting module addresses the manual, error-prone CTA process that creates ripple delays throughout trial start-up.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Slide 16 makes clear that the core problem is the manual, error-prone nature of contract execution and how those delays ripple into site activation and payment delays. The Contracting module solves this by automating the authoring, exchanging, and amending process.

questions.question: Which of the four buyer personas would be most concerned about integration headaches and audit trail compliance?
choices: Gilbert, the Clinical Operations Director
Andres, the Digital Transformation Leader
Reena, the VP IT Clinical
A fifth persona not covered in the course materials
questions.feedback_correct: Correct—Reena thinks about governance, compliance, integration that works, and audit trails that hold up under scrutiny.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Reena is the VP IT Clinical persona, and her world revolves around infrastructure, compliance risk, and integration concerns. Review Slide 5 to see how each persona's concerns differ.

questions.question: What discovery question would be most appropriate to open a conversation with Andres, the Digital Transformation Leader?
choices: How are payment delays affecting your site relationships right now?
Where are your current AI investments stalling before they reach scale?
What keeps you up at night from a compliance risk standpoint?
How many trials are you running globally each year?
questions.feedback_correct: Perfect—that question opens the door to Andres's world and lets him describe where his AI strategy is hitting friction, which is exactly where CTFS Contracting delivers value.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Different personas need different discovery questions. Slide 7 shows that Andres responds to questions about AI investments and scale, not operational pain or compliance. Use the persona-specific discovery questions from the course.

questions.question: What should you do immediately after a meaningful conversation at TechIQ?
choices: Wait until the end of the day to compile all your notes at once
Send a follow-up email within 24 hours summarizing what you discussed
Record a 90-second voice memo capturing the persona, pain, qualifying signals, and next step
Enter the contact into your CRM at the end of the event when you have time
questions.feedback_correct: Exactly right—capturing insights immediately in a 90-second memo ensures you don't lose the specific details and nuances that make follow-up personal and effective.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Waiting until later in the day causes you to lose the specific language and context the buyer used. Slide 26 emphasizes doing this immediately after each conversation, not batching it at the end.

questions.question: What is the projected annual savings for high-volume sponsors using the Contracting module?
choices: $500,000 per sponsor per year
$1.5 million per sponsor per year
$3 million per sponsor per year for sponsors running 100+ trials
Savings vary too much to project a specific number
questions.feedback_correct: That's the number—$3 million annually for high-volume sponsors, based on the cost of manual CTA re-entry, errors, and delays at scale.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Slide 19 provides a specific projection of $3 million in annual savings for sponsors running 100+ trials per year with two CTAs per site and 200 sites per trial. This number anchors the business case for enterprise-scale buyers.

questions.question: How should you respond when a buyer says, 'We already have a system in place'?
choices: Acknowledge their current system and explain why CTFS is superior
Ask what their current system does not unify, then quantify the cost of that gap
Explain that CTFS works alongside existing systems without replacing them
Pivot immediately to talking about the Contracting module as a standalone solution
questions.feedback_correct: Perfect—that approach acknowledges their reality and opens a genuine conversation about the gaps their current point solution leaves, which is where CTFS's unification value becomes clear.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Slide 23 teaches that you should not argue, but instead ask what their current system doesn't unify. This turns a potential objection into a discovery conversation that reveals real value gaps.

questions.question: According to the course, what distinguishes a qualified TechIQ lead from just a good conversation?
choices: The person is polite and engaged during your pitch
They agree to attend your company's booth at least once
They've expressed real pain, identified a decision-maker, shown openness to a demo or pilot within 30 days, or indicated budget visibility
They ask detailed technical questions about the platform architecture
questions.feedback_correct: Exactly—one of those four signals is what separates a qualified opportunity from an interesting conversation that won't turn into pipeline.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Slide 25 defines a qualified lead by specific signals: expressed pain, named decision-maker, openness to a demo/pilot within 30 days, or budget authority visibility. Engagement alone is not enough.

questions.question: Why does the course emphasize that early adoption of the Contracting module is valuable, even though it just launched?
choices: Early adopters receive a significant discount on annual licensing fees
The rest of CTFS is proven at scale, Contracting completes upstream coverage, and early adopters get input into product development
The module will become more expensive once it reaches full general availability
Competitors have already committed to the module and you'll be left behind
questions.feedback_correct: That's the value argument—the new module fills a gap in a proven platform, and early adopters have influence over its evolution.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Slide 20 provides the timing rationale: CTFS itself is proven ($15B processed, top-pharma adoption), Contracting completes the gap, and early adopters have a voice in the product roadmap. This is about strategic positioning, not price.
